questions.question: Describe the characteristics of a river's middle and lower courses and explain how meanders begin to form.
questions.expected_answer: Gentler gradient, more water from tributaries, wider deeper smoother channel, finer load in suspension; lateral erosion widens the valley; deposition forms a flood plain. Irregularities deflect flow towards one bank, which is eroded, while deposition occurs opposite; bends grow into a series of regular loops (meanders), e.g. lower Pongola, Nyl, Breede rivers.

questions.question: Explain how erosion and deposition occur on a meander and describe the resulting cross-section.
questions.expected_answer: Fastest, deepest flow (thalweg) on the outside of the bend: hydraulic action and abrasion undercut the bank, forming a river cliff. Slow, shallow water on the inside deposits sand/silt, forming a slip-off slope/point bar. Helicoidal (corkscrew) flow carries eroded material from the outer to the inner bank. Cross-section is asymmetrical: gentle inside slope, deep steep outer side. Meanders grow and migrate downstream.

questions.question: Explain the formation of an oxbow lake and the importance of oxbow lakes and meanders.
questions.expected_answer: Erosion on outer bends narrows the neck; during a flood the river breaks through (cut-off) and follows the shorter, steeper course; deposition seals the old loop, leaving a horseshoe-shaped oxbow lake, which fills with sediment and vegetation to become a marsh and then a meander scar. Importance: wetlands for wildlife (Pongola flood plain, Ndumo, over 400 bird species), flood storage, filtering water, fishing, grazing, flood-recession farming; hazards to farmland and infrastructure; channelisation increases downstream flooding, so meanders are being restored.
